title: Networking & the Web
description: Follow requests from names to validated bodies through 24 lessons, offline protocol models, an ephemeral loopback HTTP server and bounded diagnostic-client projects.
level: Foundations → intermediate practice with optional systems labs
prerequisites: Basic Python functions, lists and exceptions; vocabulary is introduced before deeper diagnosis.
Python 3.11+ and a terminal for runnable labs; no third-party package, account or external service required.
outcomes: Implement URL-origin comparisons and offline DNS expiry, then explain where an HTTP response fits in the request journey.
Run a complete ephemeral local server/client exercise and classify transport, HTTP and body outcomes.
Validate observations, cache public responses in the model and track retries against a deadline. Explain what the resulting tests establish.
Explain the difference between supplied test evidence and unexecuted deployment extensions.
setup: Download the complete practice kit and keep its files together in one directory.
Run each reference and the exact unittest command from that directory.
Use synthetic data and owned temporary resources. Read README.md for execution scope and limits.
nextSteps: Implement one explicitly identified missing boundary and add a falsifying integration test.
Record runtime, fixtures, changed contract, actual outcome and remaining limits in a review note.
Use the neighboring Python, System Design and security paths to extend the same small application without claiming professional certification.

lessons.title: 1. Follow a request through layers
lessons.takeaway: A browser action becomes a request with a destination, transport, protocol and application meaning.

sections.title: Request layers
paragraphs: A browser action becomes a request with a destination, transport, protocol and application meaning. Naming, connectivity, encryption, HTTP status and body validation can fail separately. Start with a lesson fetch: the user needs readable lesson data, not merely a socket that opened.

sections.title: Transport versus application success
paragraphs: A successful lower layer does not prove higher-layer success. A 200 response may carry malformed JSON; a correct JSON object may belong to the wrong user. Keep the stages visible in a diagnostic note so 'the network is broken' becomes a testable claim.
sections.example:
Name -> address -> connection -> TLS if HTTPS -> HTTP response -> validated lesson
Failure after HTTP 200: malformed JSON is an application observation error

exercise.prompt: Classify connection refusal versus invalid JSON.
exercise.solution: A refused connection prevents an HTTP exchange. Invalid JSON occurs after a response arrives. For a refused connection, check the server and listener configuration. For invalid JSON, compare the body with the expected response contract.
checks: Identify the last successful layer for each failure.
Give an observable signal that supports each classification.

quiz.question: Which proves a valid application result?
quiz.explanation: A connection or status code alone cannot validate application meaning and schema.

references.title: IETF RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 2. Understand addresses, ports and listeners
lessons.takeaway: An address identifies a network destination and a port selects a transport endpoint.

sections.title: Addresses and endpoints
paragraphs: An address identifies a network destination and a port selects a transport endpoint. Loopback addresses refer to the local host. Binding the lab to 127.0.0.1 prevents it intentionally listening on every interface, while port zero asks the operating system for an available port.

sections.title: Loopback listener failures
paragraphs: A listener on one port does not serve every URL. Connection refused often means no listener at that endpoint; a timeout can mean filtering, congestion or an unresponsive peer. Our lab only opens an ephemeral loopback listener and closes it through a context manager.
sections.example:
Server binds ('127.0.0.1', 0)
server.server_port gives assigned port
Client connects to that actual port
No fixed port 8000 collision required

exercise.prompt: Why should tests use the assigned port rather than assume 8000?
exercise.solution: Parallel tests or another app may occupy 8000. Port zero reserves an available endpoint and the client reads its actual assigned value.
checks: Describe how the test discovers the listener endpoint.
Explain how concurrent runs and port conflicts affect the proposed setup.

quiz.question: Which host is deliberately local here?
quiz.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is IPv4 loopback; binding there limits this listener to the local host.

references.title: Python socket
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 3. Names, records and resolver roles
lessons.takeaway: DNS relates names to typed records; a name can have more than one address and resolution can involve caching and delegation.

sections.title: DNS records and resolution
paragraphs: DNS relates names to typed records; a name can have more than one address and resolution can involve caching and delegation. An A record carries an IPv4 address, while AAAA carries IPv6. A DNS result is not a guarantee that the destination service is listening or authorized.

sections.title: The offline cache model
paragraphs: Use the supplied DnsCache as an offline lifetime model only. Its example address comes from a documentation range, not a live host. Real resolution depends on a recursive resolver, record types, answers and errors; the model does not parse packets, validate DNSSEC or simulate delegation.
sections.example:
lessons.example -> A 192.0.2.10
Name resolution succeeds
Port 443 can still refuse a connection
These are separate observations

exercise.prompt: Which evidence would distinguish name failure from HTTP 404?
exercise.solution: A resolver error happens before an HTTP response; 404 means a server responded to the request. Capture the stage and actual error category.
checks: Provide the resolver and HTTP evidence needed for the comparison.
State which layer each observation can and cannot establish.

quiz.question: Does an A record prove HTTPS is working?
options: No, it only provides an address mapping
quiz.explanation: An address record does not establish listener, TLS identity or application behavior.

references.title: IETF RFC 1035: DNS
references.section: Sections 3.2.1–3.2.2: resource record format and types
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 4. TTL and stale DNS observations
lessons.takeaway: A TTL limits how long a DNS answer may be retained under the resolver's rules.

sections.title: Expiry and new resolution
paragraphs: A TTL limits how long a DNS answer may be retained under the resolver's rules. Our simplified cache stores an expiry and returns no answer at or after it. An expired value needs a new resolution, which can produce a changed address or a failure.

In real DNS, a record with TTL 0 may still be used for the current transaction; it must not be reused from cache for later requests. This teaching cache models reuse only, so its immediate lookup returns no cached answer.

sections.title: DNS versus connection lifetime
paragraphs: A small TTL does not migrate an already-open connection and is not a universal failover promise. DNS caches, connection reuse and application state have different lifetimes. The reference injects now so the exact boundary is deterministic, not a test that sleeps for five seconds.
sections.example:
Remember at t=10 with TTL=5
lookup(14.99) -> old address
lookup(15) -> None
Re-resolution must be a separate step

exercise.prompt: Add a test that stores an entry with TTL 0 and looks it up at the same time. Predict the result before running it.
exercise.solution: An entry stored with a zero TTL expires immediately in this model. A lookup at the insertion time returns None. Test both operations with the same injected time, without sleeping.
checks: Specify a clock, insertion time and lookup time.
Record the expected lookup outcome and justify it from the expiry rule.

quiz.question: At t=15, which result matches the model?
options: Return the old address until a new one is explicitly inserted
Return the old address once more because expiry comparisons use greater-than only
quiz.explanation: This model expires the entry at now equal to its expiry; it does not keep stale data indefinitely.

references.title: IETF RFC 1035: DNS
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 5. TCP streams and message boundaries
lessons.takeaway: TCP exposes an ordered byte stream while a connection is healthy; one write is not promised to equal one read.

sections.title: Byte streams and framing
paragraphs: TCP exposes an ordered byte stream while a connection is healthy. One write need not match one read. The application protocol defines message boundaries. HTTP framing identifies where headers and content end, so a single packet cannot establish that a message is complete.

sections.title: Bounded and truncated reads
paragraphs: Use the standard HTTP client rather than writing a partial TCP parser for this course. A read can yield fewer bytes than requested, and a peer can close halfway through content. Bounded reads protect the application from accepting unlimited bodies, but correct handling must also recognize truncated messages.
sections.example:
Server sends 20 bytes in two writes
Receiver reads 8 then 12
Same content, different chunking
A one-read parser would silently truncate

sections.title: Frame bytes before decoding text
paragraphs: The word cafe with an accented final letter needs two UTF-8 bytes for that letter. A recv boundary can separate those bytes; decoding each chunk independently can therefore fail even though the complete message is valid. Accumulate bytes until the application delimiter arrives, enforce a size limit and only then decode the complete frame. A sendall call does not reserve a matching recv call.

tcp_framing.py uses a real loopback listener and deliberately small three-byte reads. One exchange splits a UTF-8 character across sends; another sends two newline-delimited frames together. Both must yield complete messages. EOF with remaining bytes is an incomplete frame, not a successful short message. This tiny newline protocol teaches TCP framing; it is not an HTTP parser.
sections.example:
wire bytes: b'caf\xc3' + b'\xa9\nsecond\n'
frames: ['café', 'second']
wire bytes: b'incomplete' then EOF -> error, no completed frame

exercise.prompt: Run python tcp_framing.py. Change the malformed fixture from an incomplete frame to 65 bytes without a newline. Which boundary should reject it and why should more reads not be required?
checks: Both valid exchanges produce two messages regardless of send/read chunking.
The 65-byte frame exceeds the 64-byte limit; incomplete EOF is separately rejected.
exercise.solution: The pending-frame size check rejects the 65th byte before allowing unbounded accumulation. EOF with fewer bytes but no delimiter is a different error: the protocol frame never completed. Neither failure should publish a fabricated complete message. A decoder must bound memory as well as recognize message boundaries.

quiz.question: Why is one socket read insufficient as a general parser?
options: Stream chunks need not match messages
A successful sendall forces the peer to return exactly that many bytes in its next recv
Receiving fewer bytes than requested always means the peer has finished its message
quiz.explanation: TCP is a stream: reads may split or combine application messages.

lessons.title: 6. Parse a URL and its origin
lessons.takeaway: A URL contains scheme, authority, path, query and sometimes a fragment.

sections.title: URL parts and origins
paragraphs: A URL contains scheme, authority, path, query and sometimes a fragment. An origin is the scheme, host and port tuple used by browser security rules. Our origin helper normalizes the host and default port and rejects embedded credentials or fragments as an explicit lab request policy.

sections.title: Parsing versus permission
paragraphs: Parsing is not full validation or authorization. A syntactically acceptable HTTPS URL could point to an internal resource in a server-side fetcher. Fragments identify client-side locations and are not sent as the HTTP request target. Do not concatenate untrusted strings into URLs without understanding encoding.
sections.example:
https://EXAMPLE.test/a?q=1 -> ('https','example.test',443)
http://example.test -> ('http','example.test',80)
Different scheme means different origin

exercise.prompt: Compare https://example.test and https://example.test:444.
exercise.solution: Their ports differ, so their origins differ. A path change on the same scheme, host and port keeps the origin unchanged.
checks: List the parsed components used in each origin comparison.
Justify the comparison using the origin definition.

quiz.question: Which changes the origin?
quiz.explanation: Origin includes scheme, host and port; changing only the path or fragment does not alter it.

references.title: Python urllib.parse
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 7. Decode bytes at a named boundary
lessons.takeaway: A response body arrives as bytes.

sections.title: Bytes, text and JSON
paragraphs: A response body arrives as bytes. Text decoding and JSON parsing are separate transformations; content type tells the client how the representation is intended to be interpreted. RFC 8259 requires UTF-8 for JSON exchanged between systems outside a closed ecosystem, and malformed encodings must not quietly become valid-looking lesson content.

sections.title: Decoding and byte length
paragraphs: The supplied decoder first decodes bytes as strict UTF-8, then passes the resulting text to Python's JSON reader. It rejects decoding and syntax failures. Passing bytes directly to json.loads would also accept UTF-16 and UTF-32, which is broader than this lab's wire contract. It also checks a strict schema after parsing. Do not measure Content-Length from characters: a non-ASCII lesson name can require more bytes. Compression and transfer framing are separate protocol concerns delegated to the chosen client stack.
sections.example:
Text lesson='café'
UTF-8 bytes contain more octets than text characters
Wrong encoding or truncated bytes -> decoding failure
Correct bytes + wrong field types -> schema failure

sections.title: Try bytes before the full decoder
paragraphs: Use a Python prompt for this first check. Encode the text cafe with an accented final letter, then decode those bytes back to text. The round trip is about encoding; it says nothing yet about JSON syntax or a lesson schema. body-contracts later connects all three checks.

exercise.prompt: In Python, compare len("café") with len("café".encode("utf-8")). Then try b"\xff".decode("utf-8"). Which transformation fails?
exercise.solution: The text has four characters and its UTF-8 representation has five bytes. Decoding b"\xff" raises UnicodeDecodeError. No JSON parser or remote server is needed. Later, body-contracts wraps this failure as ProtocolError.
checks: Keep byte count distinct from character count.
Locate the malformed input failure at decoding, before JSON or schema checks.

quiz.question: What should an invalid byte sequence become?
quiz.explanation: Invalid encoded content cannot be published as a valid lesson; the observation decoder rejects it.

references.section: Sections 8.3 and 8.4: media type and content encoding
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

references.title: IETF RFC 8259: JSON
references.scope: RFC 8259 requires UTF-8 outside closed ecosystems. This lab deliberately accepts only UTF-8 and rejects other encodings.

lessons.title: 8. Read methods, fields and content
lessons.takeaway: An HTTP request has a method and target plus fields and optional content.

sections.title: Request and response structure
paragraphs: An HTTP request has a method and target plus fields and optional content. A response has a status and fields plus permitted content. Treat field names case-insensitively at a real boundary, and keep content type separate from the bytes themselves. The local server serves a tiny JSON lesson with an explicit byte length.

sections.title: Content length and HEAD
paragraphs: Content-Length counts octets, not characters or JSON entries. HEAD describes the representation without sending its body; it is useful for metadata but does not validate a GET body. Our local reference uses the Python server/client libraries for framing, not a complete teaching implementation of HTTP parsing.
sections.example:
GET /lesson -> 200, Content-Type application/json, body bytes
HEAD /lesson -> 200, same representation length, empty body

exercise.prompt: Why calculate Content-Length from encoded bytes?
exercise.solution: Non-ASCII characters can occupy multiple bytes, so len(text) can differ from len(text.encode('utf-8')). A wrong length breaks framing.
checks: Provide a non-ASCII message and measure its encoded payload.
Compare the declared length with the bytes actually sent.

quiz.question: For HEAD, what should the lab client receive?
quiz.explanation: HEAD returns representation metadata without the representation body.

references.title: IETF RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
references.section: Sections 6 and 9.3.2: message abstraction and HEAD
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 9. Interpret status without overclaiming
lessons.takeaway: Status codes describe HTTP response semantics.

sections.title: Response semantics
paragraphs: Status codes describe HTTP response semantics. A successful representation response, a missing route and an unavailable service require different client actions. Our synthetic server exposes 200, 401, 404 and 503 deliberately. A response status says nothing by itself about whether returned JSON satisfies the app schema.

sections.title: Status and body handling
paragraphs: Separate status handling from body parsing. Retrying every 4xx can repeat a client mistake, while retrying 503 indefinitely can amplify an outage. The lab decoder accepts only the intended 200 lesson contract; that narrow decision is local application policy rather than a generic HTTP library rule.
sections.example:
/lesson -> 200 lesson
/private without cookie -> 401 synthetic denial
/missing -> 404
/unavailable -> 503
/bad-json -> 200 but decoder rejects

exercise.prompt: Does a 404 identify a DNS failure?
exercise.solution: No. A 404 is an HTTP response from a server or intermediary, not a DNS error. Check the target or route and which component answered. It does not prove a fresh DNS lookup occurred: the client may use a literal IP address, a cached answer, an existing connection or a proxy.
checks: Identify the evidence supplied by the response and the layer that produced it.
Explain what additional observation would support a name-resolution diagnosis.

quiz.question: Which observation belongs after the HTTP layer?
quiz.explanation: Body validation follows transport and HTTP status processing.

references.title: IETF RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 10. Safety, idempotency and retry decisions
lessons.takeaway: A safe method requests a read-oriented operation according to HTTP semantics; idempotency concerns the intended effect of repeating a request.

sections.title: Safety and repeated effects
paragraphs: A safe method requests a read-oriented operation according to HTTP semantics; idempotency concerns the intended effect of repeating a request. GET and HEAD are good candidates for a bounded read retry policy. That does not make a badly designed endpoint immune to effects or remove traffic costs.

sections.title: A bounded read-retry policy
paragraphs: POST is not generically idempotent. A server may implement an operation key that makes a particular POST safely repeatable, but the client needs that actual contract. Our simple policy retries only GET or HEAD and only with attempts and time remaining. It does not establish application idempotency.
sections.example:
GET attempt 1 of 3 with 1s remaining -> retry allowed
POST attempt 1 -> denied by local policy
GET attempt 3 -> no remaining attempt

exercise.prompt: How should a booking client handle a lost POST response?
exercise.solution: Use the booking API's documented operation identity and reconciliation semantics; do not assume failure means no booking. The local read-only retry helper is insufficient.
checks: List the possible server outcomes after the response is lost.
Specify how the client resolves uncertainty and bounds further effects.

quiz.question: Which provides the missing duplicate-effect protection for retrying an uncertain POST, once retryability and attempt/time budgets are also satisfied?
options: A timeout after the request was sent
A documented deduplication contract for that operation
An HTTP 5xx response regardless of the endpoint contract
quiz.explanation: An uncertain POST needs its operation-specific deduplication contract; a timeout alone is insufficient.

references.title: IETF RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 11. TLS protects a transport boundary
lessons.takeaway: TLS authenticates peers under its configuration and protects transport confidentiality and integrity.

sections.title: Transport protection
paragraphs: TLS authenticates peers under its configuration and protects transport confidentiality and integrity. HTTPS combines HTTP with TLS; it does not prove the application authorizes a resource or validates its own data. A trusted certificate must also match the requested server name for ordinary HTTPS identity checks.

sections.title: What the loopback lab tests
paragraphs: Our lab uses plain loopback HTTP and does not perform a TLS handshake. The test inspects a default client's certificate-required and hostname-check settings only. Do not label those configuration assertions as encrypted-network evidence or disable verification merely to make an exercise connect.
sections.example:
Valid chain + wrong hostname -> reject in a correctly configured HTTPS client
Valid HTTPS + invalid lesson JSON -> decoder still rejects
Local HTTP lab -> no transport encryption

exercise.prompt: What would a real local TLS extension require? Optional live drill: practice/browser-boundary-drill.md; record browser/TLS observations separately.
exercise.solution: Create a test CA and server certificate, then configure client trust. Check that the matching host succeeds and that a wrong hostname or untrusted chain fails. Inspect the negotiated transport. Keep it separate from the current HTTP evidence.
checks: List setup and runtime observations required for a TLS experiment.
Separate certificate configuration from verified client behavior.

quiz.question: What does a TLS configuration test prove here?
quiz.explanation: The test checks context settings only; no certificate or handshake was exchanged.

references.title: IETF RFC 8446: TLS 1.3
references.section: Sections 4.4 and 7: authentication and cryptographic computation
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 12. Inspect trust configuration without bypasses
lessons.takeaway: Certificate trust is configured by a client's trust roots and verification policy.

sections.title: Trust roots and hostname checks
paragraphs: Certificate trust is configured by a client's trust roots and verification policy. Python's create_default_context enables certificate verification and hostname checking for a client-oriented context. Its supported protocol details also depend on the linked TLS library; record the runtime if testing real connections.

sections.title: Diagnosing certificate failures
paragraphs: Never turn off checks to hide an unknown certificate error in a production-style recommendation. Diagnose name mismatch, trust-chain issues and time validity separately. This reference deliberately does not generate certificates or reach the public internet, so certificate-expiry and handshake-failure drills are design extensions.
sections.example:
context = ssl.create_default_context()
context.verify_mode == CERT_REQUIRED
context.check_hostname is True
No network exchange has occurred

exercise.prompt: What do these passing assertions establish?
exercise.solution: The default context requires identity checks. No server certificate was presented and no encrypted session was established; a handshake test remains unexecuted.
checks: Attach each proposed claim to a named executed assertion.
List TLS properties that remain unobserved by the local fixture.

quiz.question: What would disabling hostname checking weaken?
quiz.explanation: Hostname checking verifies the requested server identity against the presented certificate.

references.title: Python ssl
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 13. Cookies add state with explicit scope
lessons.takeaway: A server uses Set-Cookie to ask a user agent to retain a name/value and attributes; later requests may send matching Cookie values.

sections.title: Scoped browser state
paragraphs: A server uses Set-Cookie to ask a user agent to retain a name/value and attributes; later requests may send matching Cookie values. Cookies are scoped state, not proof of identity by themselves. The lab issues a visibly synthetic session token and checks it on one private route to demonstrate transport mechanics.

sections.title: The synthetic cookie boundary
paragraphs: HttpOnly limits script access, while Secure requires secure transport under user-agent rules. The lab runs HTTP, so it deliberately does not claim a Secure-cookie authentication design. The synthetic token is fixed and forgeable. Production sessions need real authentication, unpredictable identifiers and server-side authorization.
sections.example:
GET /cookie -> Set-Cookie: session=synthetic; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
GET /private without cookie -> 401
Cookie: session=synthetic -> local demonstration 200

exercise.prompt: Why is the lab cookie not a security boundary?
exercise.solution: Its fixed value is known to every learner and the server has no real identity service. It demonstrates header flow, not authenticated accounts.
checks: Describe who can supply or alter the lab cookie value.
State what evidence would be required for a security claim.

quiz.question: What does HttpOnly chiefly restrict?
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly restricts script access to a cookie; it is not general cross-site or authorization protection.

references.title: IETF RFC 6265: HTTP State Management
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 14. CORS and browser-specific enforcement
lessons.takeaway: An origin policy and CORS affect how browsers expose cross-origin responses to scripts.

sections.title: Cross-origin response access
paragraphs: An origin policy and CORS affect how browsers expose cross-origin responses to scripts. CORS is not a general network firewall: non-browser clients can send requests regardless of browser response-exposure rules. Server authorization must independently decide whether an actor can access a resource.

sections.title: Python versus browser enforcement
paragraphs: The Python HTTP client does not implement browser CORS enforcement. Seeing it read a response does not prove a browser script can read that response. Some requests trigger preflight, and credentials add requirements. Keep credentials and allowed origins narrowly scoped when designing a real extension.
sections.example:
Browser page origin A fetches API origin B
Server returns no appropriate CORS permission
Browser script may be denied response access
Python client is not that browser

exercise.prompt: Would adding Access-Control-Allow-Origin authorize a private booking? Optional live drill: practice/browser-boundary-drill.md; record browser/TLS observations separately.
exercise.solution: No. It changes browser exposure policy; authentication and object-level authorization remain separate server checks. Specify them separately in tests.
checks: Identify the browser and server decisions involved in the request.
Propose independent allowed and denied cases with observable outcomes.

quiz.question: Why can a Python client read an otherwise CORS-blocked body?
options: It is not enforcing the browser CORS protocol
The server has no private data
quiz.explanation: A Python HTTP client does not apply browser CORS response-exposure rules.

references.title: WHATWG Fetch Standard
references.scope: Network and HTTP concepts with Python 3.11+ examples. The practice guide separates local tests from browser and live-network checks.

lessons.title: 15. Freshness, reuse and storage permission
lessons.takeaway: An HTTP cache can store a response and decide when it is fresh enough to reuse under the applicable rules.

sections.title: Freshness and storage rules
paragraphs: An HTTP cache can store a response and decide when it is fresh enough to reuse under the applicable rules. max-age describes a freshness lifetime; no-store directs caches not to store, while unqualified private forbids a shared cache from storing the response but permits private-cache storage under the other applicable rules. Our SharedCache is a deliberately small offline model with an explicit private flag.

sections.title: Shared-cache exclusions and limits
paragraphs: Do not infer cacheability from status alone. User-specific output and public lesson data require different keys and storage policy. The reference is not a parser for every Cache-Control directive; it demonstrates that private content stays out of the shared map and that expiry is tested with an injected time. The offline cache omits Vary, Age, revalidation and full directive parsing; those need separate protocol tests before it could be a real HTTP cache.
sections.example:
Store public lesson at 10 with max_age 5
get at 14 -> body
get at 15 -> miss
private=True -> nothing stored

exercise.prompt: Why is a URL-only shared key unsafe for personalized output?
exercise.solution: Different accounts may request the same URL and receive different representations. Prefer no-store for this exercise; real caching needs explicit partition and variation policy.
checks: Provide two requests whose outputs differ under the same URL.
Evaluate whether the proposed cache key keeps their results separate.

quiz.question: Which is stronger than merely requiring revalidation?
quiz.explanation: no-store forbids storage, while revalidation rules permit storage under conditions.

lessons.title: 16. Conditional requests and 304 responses
lessons.takeaway: A validator lets a client ask whether its stored representation still matches the server's current one.

sections.title: Representation validators
paragraphs: A validator lets a client ask whether its stored representation still matches the server's current one. Our fixed lesson ETag and If-None-Match produce a 304 response when they match. The client must already have a suitable representation to reuse; 304 does not deliver a new lesson body.

sections.title: Reusing a stored response
paragraphs: The lab's ETag is a teaching constant for an immutable sample. A changing application must update validators with the representation and respect variation and cache rules. Compare bytes and metadata deliberately; do not parse an empty 304 body as newly returned JSON.
sections.example:
First GET -> 200 with ETag '"lesson-v1"'
Conditional GET with same value -> 304, no body
Client reuses its stored lesson

exercise.prompt: What should a client without a cached body do on unexpected 304?
exercise.solution: Treat its local state as insufficient and recover with an appropriate unconditional request under the application policy. Do not publish an empty lesson.
checks: Specify the client state before receiving the response.
Define the next request and the conditions for publishing a result.

quiz.question: Where does the body after a legitimate 304 come from?
options: The 304 response body after JSON decoding
A fresh representation generated from the ETag value
quiz.explanation: A 304 validates an existing stored representation and does not supply a new body.

lessons.title: 17. Follow redirects with a policy
lessons.takeaway: A redirect describes another target; deciding to follow it belongs to the client's policy.

sections.title: Redirect targets and methods
paragraphs: A redirect describes another target; deciding to follow it belongs to the client's policy. The lab observes a 307 and relative Location without automatically following. For 307, the method is preserved when a client redirects. Redirect chains still need bounds and destination validation.

sections.title: Policy at every hop
paragraphs: A redirect can cross origins or lead from a permitted public target to an internal service in a server-side fetcher. Reapply destination and credential-forwarding policy at each hop. Never assume a successful first target makes every later Location safe. Keep observations and followed results distinct in diagnostics.
sections.example:
GET /redirect -> 307, Location /lesson
Lab result is the redirect itself
Optional follow -> validate resolved target, count hop, GET /lesson

exercise.prompt: What must a bounded redirect helper track?
exercise.solution: Check the hop count, the resolved destination origin, the method rules and whether credentials may be forwarded. Stop loops and reject destinations outside the client policy.
checks: Provide a redirect chain and explicit stopping conditions.
Demonstrate behavior for a loop and a destination outside the allowed boundary.

quiz.question: What does the supplied fetch do with 307?
quiz.explanation: fetch returns the redirect status and Location; following requires a separate bounded policy.

lessons.title: 18. Forward proxies, reverse proxies and trust
lessons.takeaway: A forward proxy acts for clients; a reverse proxy or gateway faces clients on behalf of an origin service.

sections.title: Proxy roles and metadata
paragraphs: A forward proxy acts for clients; a reverse proxy or gateway faces clients on behalf of an origin service. Each hop can alter routing, buffering, TLS termination and timeout behavior. An origin may receive a proxy's connection rather than the browser's, so forwarded metadata needs a trusted boundary.

sections.title: Trusted forwarding boundaries
paragraphs: The loopback reference has no proxy. Do not trust an arbitrary client-supplied forwarding field as proof of identity or IP policy. A real deployment must define which intermediary may set it and how spoofed incoming fields are removed. Diagnose status origin before blaming the application.
sections.example:
Browser -> edge proxy (TLS terminates) -> origin HTTP
Proxy times out waiting -> 504 to browser
Origin might still be computing; no rollback implied

exercise.prompt: What should be verified for a forwarded client-IP policy? Optional live drill: practice/browser-boundary-drill.md; record browser/TLS observations separately.
exercise.solution: Only configured proxies may supply authoritative forwarding metadata; direct client values are rejected or ignored. Test spoofed fields and document the connection trust boundary.
checks: Describe the trusted proxy boundary and the source of each forwarded value.
Include a spoofed-header case and specify its observable policy outcome.

quiz.question: Can a proxy timeout prove the origin did nothing?
options: No, work may still be running
Only if the response body is empty
quiz.explanation: A caller-facing proxy timeout does not prove the origin stopped processing.

lessons.title: 19. Distinguish waits and overall deadlines
lessons.takeaway: A timeout bounds a particular wait under a library's semantics; an overall deadline limits how long the application is willing to keep trying.

sections.title: Waits and overall deadlines
paragraphs: A timeout bounds a particular wait under a library's semantics; an overall deadline limits how long the application is willing to keep trying. DNS, connection, TLS, response headers and content reads may have different wait points. A caller timeout does not cancel remote effects automatically.

sections.title: A controlled read timeout
paragraphs: The /stall endpoint waits on an Event before sending a response. A client with a short socket timeout should stop waiting; cleanup releases the server event afterward. This controlled local read timeout is real, while injected-clock retry tests model a separate policy. Avoid treating either as internet latency benchmarking.
sections.example:
Server signals request started
Client waits for headers with timeout .15s
Client gets TimeoutError
Cleanup releases server; request did reach it

sections.title: A read timeout can reset while the overall budget expires
paragraphs: Suppose a server sends one byte every 80 ms and the socket timeout is 100 ms. Every individual read may succeed indefinitely. A two-second request deadline must instead use a monotonic start time and subtract elapsed time before each wait. Retrying with a fresh two-second budget on every attempt defeats the caller's total budget.

With a two-second budget, an initial attempt using 1.4 seconds and a planned 0.4-second backoff leave only 0.2 seconds. A second two-second attempt is inconsistent with that contract. Bound its wait by the remaining time or decline the retry. A timeout after a POST still leaves the outcome uncertain; deadline arithmetic does not provide idempotency or remotely undo a committed write.
sections.example:
total budget 2.0s - attempt 1.4s - backoff 0.4s = 0.2s remaining
next wait <= 0.2s; no fresh full budget
received response prefix != complete application result

exercise.prompt: A peer sends a byte every 80 ms under a 100 ms read timeout. Explain why the client can exceed a two-second goal, and calculate the remaining attempt budget after 1.4 seconds plus 0.4 seconds backoff.
checks: Per-read progress can keep avoiding the socket timeout while total duration grows.
The next attempt has at most 0.2 seconds, and an uncertain earlier write must not be blindly repeated.
exercise.solution: The timeout bounds an individual blocking read, not the full exchange. Use one monotonic deadline across reads, backoff and attempts. Only 0.2 seconds remains; skip a retry that cannot usefully finish or cap its waits accordingly. For a mutating request also resolve idempotency/outcome uncertainty.

quiz.question: What does client timeout establish?
options: The caller stopped waiting at that boundary
Remote work was forcibly rolled back
quiz.explanation: The caller stops waiting at the timed boundary; remote effects are not forcibly undone.

lessons.title: 20. Bound retries by attempts and time
lessons.takeaway: Repeated reads can recover a transient failure, but every retry adds load.

sections.title: Retry load and budgets
paragraphs: Repeated reads can recover a transient failure, but every retry adds load. The advanced reference bounds GET attempts and checks an injected overall deadline before dispatch. It retries selected gateway/unavailable statuses and returns the final status with minimal attempt metadata.

sections.title: Bounding each callback
paragraphs: The reference call must itself be bounded by a transport timeout; the helper cannot preempt a blocked callback. It has no backoff or jitter and performs no real retries against a service by default. A deployment extension needs retry timing, per-attempt budget, cancellation and coordination with existing retry layers.
sections.example:
503,503,503 with max_attempts=3 -> stop at three calls
Clock already beyond deadline -> zero new calls
503 then 200 -> success on attempt two

exercise.prompt: Three nested layers each allow three total attempts, including the original. Calculate the maximum deepest calls. Then compare a single retry owner allowing three attempts.
exercise.solution: The nested policies can make 3 * 3 * 3 = 27 deepest calls. A single owner making three attempts against a callee that does not retry makes at most three. These maxima assume every attempt reaches the next layer and the deadline permits them.
checks: Count attempts including the original explicitly.
Explain why the shared deadline can reduce the maximum.

quiz.question: Which prevents a new call after time is exhausted?
quiz.explanation: Checking before dispatch prevents a new attempt when the overall budget is already exhausted.

lessons.title: 21. Validate response bodies after transport
lessons.takeaway: A client should bound content and validate media type, syntax and application schema.

sections.title: Media type, syntax and schema
paragraphs: A client should bound content and validate media type, syntax and application schema. The lesson decoder expects a JSON object with string lesson and exact integer version. It rejects malformed JSON, unknown fields and booleans where a numeric version is intended. Transport success is only the start.

sections.title: Malformed and oversized bodies
paragraphs: An error page can arrive with 200, and a valid JSON object can have incompatible fields. Preserve the distinction between HTTP errors and protocol/application observation errors. The reference's 4096-byte bound is a teaching limit chosen for this small representation; state it in the contract and test oversized input.
sections.example:
200 + application/json + {broken -> ProtocolError
200 + text/html + expected-looking bytes -> ProtocolError
200 + {"lesson":"http","version":true} -> ProtocolError

exercise.prompt: Add an oversized-body assertion.
exercise.solution: Supply more than 4096 bytes to the decoder and assert ProtocolError. For streaming extensions, enforce the bound during reading before accumulating the whole body.
checks: Specify an input at and beyond the configured size limit.
Verify both the reported failure and absence of a published result on rejection.

quiz.question: What should happen to a malformed 200 response?
options: Reject it at the body contract boundary
quiz.explanation: A malformed successful-status observation must fail schema/syntax validation before publication.

lessons.title: 22. Build a layered incident timeline
lessons.takeaway: A good network diagnosis reports which stage completed, what failed and the relevant bounded metadata.

sections.title: Layered incident evidence
paragraphs: Identify which request stage completed and which failed. Record the request ID, status, attempt number and timings without copying cookies or full bodies. Compare client and server observations. A client timeout can occur even when the server completes the work.

sections.title: Correlation without credentials
paragraphs: Use a controlled case to test a hypothesis before changing every timeout. The lab's trace contains attempt and status only; it is not distributed tracing. A real system must propagate safe correlation and distinguish proxy, origin and client events. Do not log credentials to make a reproduction easier.
sections.example:
Client attempt 1 -> 503
Client attempt 2 -> 200
Trace: [{attempt:1,status:503},{attempt:2,status:200}]
No Cookie or private body retained

exercise.prompt: What evidence separates a proxy 504 from an origin 500?
exercise.solution: Compare proxy and origin logs using their timestamps and request identifiers, then inspect the response metadata. A single browser status cannot establish where processing failed.
checks: Collect timestamped client, proxy and origin observations.
Explain which observations distinguish the two proposed failure sources.

quiz.question: Which diagnostic field should be excluded?
quiz.explanation: Cookies carry sensitive session state and should not be copied into diagnostic events.

lessons.title: 23. Keep semantics separate from HTTP version
lessons.takeaway: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry related HTTP semantics through different wire protocols and transports.

sections.title: HTTP semantics and wire protocols
paragraphs: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry related HTTP semantics through different wire protocols and transports. Applications should rely on the method, status and representation contract instead of assuming packet shape or one connection per request. The stdlib lab explicitly exercises HTTP/1.1 only.

sections.title: HTTP/1.1 evidence limits
paragraphs: Do not call a local HTTP/1.1 result evidence for multiplexing, QUIC or proxy compatibility. Compare repeated representation outcomes when extending to another client/server stack, while measuring protocol-specific behavior separately. Header normalization and framing decisions belong to the actual protocol implementation.
sections.example:
Same application contract: GET lesson -> 200 JSON
Current lab: HTTP/1.1 over loopback TCP
Unexecuted extension: same contract over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3

exercise.prompt: Which claims need new experiments for HTTP/3?
exercise.solution: Negotiation, connection migration and transport behavior need a suitable implementation and controlled network tests. Existing JSON-schema checks remain useful but do not establish them.
checks: Map each proposed protocol claim to a separate observable experiment.
State which current fixture results transfer and which require new evidence.

quiz.question: What is verified by this lab?
quiz.explanation: The actual server/client pair uses HTTP/1.1; other transport claims require other implementations.

lessons.title: 24. Defend a client with explicit evidence
lessons.takeaway: The final project combines URL policy, observed HTTP semantics, validated bodies, public-cache isolation and bounded reads.

sections.title: Client requirements and evidence
paragraphs: The final project combines URL policy, observed HTTP semantics, validated bodies, public-cache isolation and bounded reads. An evidence table should link each requirement to a fixture and actual result. Keep an unexecuted extension list for real DNS, TLS, browser cookies, CORS and intermediary behavior.

sections.title: Unexecuted network extensions
paragraphs: Passing local tests makes a useful baseline, not a complete production client. The synthetic cookie is not authentication, cache models do not implement the full RFC, and the retry helper needs bounded callbacks. A review should name these boundaries so another learner knows what to implement next.
sections.example:
Claim: private data never enters shared model cache -> private-flag test
Claim: malformed lesson rejected -> /bad-json integration test
Unknown: real certificate validation -> separate TLS drill

exercise.prompt: Choose the smallest next experiment before using real HTTPS.
exercise.solution: Create a local test CA and server. Check that a trusted certificate with a matching name succeeds, and that an untrusted certificate or wrong name fails without disabling verification. Retain the existing body and timeout contracts.
checks: Name the unresolved claim and the smallest discriminating experiment.
Specify expected observations, stopping conditions and remaining limitations.

quiz.question: Which review claim is supported today?
options: The client's browser security is certified
Controlled loopback and offline model behaviors passed
quiz.explanation: The suite supplies controlled loopback and model evidence, not browser or remote security certification.
